extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates or graduate students studying commutative algebra; readers of a commutative-algebra textbook
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of textbook propositions, lemmas and exercise statements (with hints/solutions) on ideals, prime ideals, radicals, polynomial and power-series rings, and the prime spectrum (Spec) with Zariski topology. Intended as exercises and worked hints for learners of commutative algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3 (1.11i): Ideal not contained in any prime not contained in union
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A be a ring, let a be an ideal, and let p1, . . . , pn, n ≥ 1 be prime ideals. If a is not contained in any pi, then a is not contained in their union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof construct elements a1,...,an in a with ai ∈ pi \ ⋃_{j≠i} pj and form a := a1·...·a_{n−1} + an which lies in a but not in any pi. (This is a standard finite-prime-avoidance argument; used as a weaker form sufficient for many purposes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 4 (1.11ii): Primes contain products ⇒ contain a factor
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is a prime ideal containing ∏_{i=1}^n a_i then p ⊃ a_i for some i. If p = ∏ a_i then p = a_i for some i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the ideal-version of primality: p ⊃ ab ⇒ p ⊃ a or p ⊃ b, extended inductively to finite products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic quotient-ideal identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: (1 : b) = (1) = (a : 0) and (a : 1) = a. If a ⊂ a', b ⊂ b' then (a : b) ⊂ (a' : b').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are fundamental identities for colon (quotient) ideals; used to manipulate annihilators and quotient-ideal relations in exercises (see Exercise 1.12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise 1.12: Colon-ideal identities and relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements include (i) a ⊂ (a : b); (ii) (a : b)b ⊂ a; (iii) ((a : b) : c) = (a : bc) = ((a : c) : b); (iv) (⋂_i ai : b) = ⋂_i (ai : b); (v) (a : ⋂_i bi) = ⋂_i (a : bi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solutions left to the reader; comments show inclusions can be strict in general with explicit counterexamples using polynomial quotient maps. Useful caution: many natural inclusions are strict unless extra hypotheses hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of the radical r(a) (Exercise 1.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) r(a) ⊃ a; (ii) r(r(a)) = r(a); (iii) r(ab) = r(a ∩ b) = r(a) ∩ r(b); (iv) r(a) = (1) ⇐⇒ a = (1); (v) r(a + b) = r(r(a) + r(b)); (vi) if p is prime, r(p^n) = p for all n>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard properties of radicals; proofs are left to the reader but referenced as routine consequences of prime-ideal characterizations of radicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension (ae) of an ideal along a ring morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: If f: A → B is a ring morphism and a an ideal of A, define ae := (f(α) | α ∈ a) (the ideal generated by images).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to define contraction/extension behavior; many properties and (in)equalities relating ae to sums, intersections, products, quotients and radicals are given in Exercise 1.18 with explicit examples showing strict inclusions are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise 1.18: Behavior of extension under operations (sums, intersections, products, quotients, radicals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various relations such as (a1 + a2)e = a1e + a2e, (a1 ∩ a2)e ⊂ a1e ∩ a2e, (a1a2)e = a1e · a2e, (a1 : a2)e ⊂ (a1e : a2e), and r(a)e ⊂ r(ae).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints and multiple counterexamples are provided demonstrating that inclusions can be strict. The text gives concrete polynomial-ring examples illustrating each strictness phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nilpotents and units (Exercise 1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x is nilpotent in A then 1 + x is a unit of A. Consequently, the sum of a nilpotent element and a unit is a unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via geometric series: (1 − x)^{-1} = ∑_{n≥0} x^n when x^N = 0 for some N. Standard lemma used frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Units, nilpotents and zero-divisors in A[x] (Exercise 1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) f ∈ A[x] is a unit ⇐⇒ a0 is a unit in A and a1,...,an are nilpotent; (ii) f is nilpotent ⇐⇒ all coefficients are nilpotent; (iii) f is a zero-divisor ⇐⇒ there exists a ≠ 0 in A such that a f = 0; (iv) primitivity: f g primitive ⇐⇒ f and g primitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use degree-minimal annihilators and reduction modulo primes. Part (i) uses induction on degrees of inverse polynomial; (iii) uses minimal-degree argument to force coefficient annihilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multivariable polynomial generalization (Exercise 1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizes Exercise 1.2 to A[x1,...,xr]: units ⇐⇒ constant term unit and all nonconstant-monomial coefficients nilpotent; nilpotent ⇐⇒ all coefficients nilpotent; primitivity criterion for product holds similarly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use specialization to A/p and reductions to one-variable cases; arguments rely on arbitrary prime ideals p of A and their behavior under reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annihilator descent / zero-divisors in polynomial rings (Exercise 1.3iii, Lemmas 5 & 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ A[x1,...,xp] has a nonzero annihilator in A[x1,...,xp+q] then f has a nonzero annihilator in A (more precisely in fewer-variable polynomial rings down to A). Equivalently, a nonzero zero-divisor in A[x1,...,xn] has a nonzero annihilator in A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs: (1) use minimal-degree annihilator in one variable and argue coefficientwise (Lemma 5); (2) use graded-lex monomial order and minimal multi-degree annihilator. Both force existence of coefficient in A annihilating f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobson radical in A[x] equals nilradical (Exercise 1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the ring A[x], the Jacobson radical equals the nilradical (R(A[x]) = r(A[x]) ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch: if f is in Jacobson radical, then 1 − x f is a unit (Prop.1.9) so coefficients are nilpotent by Exercise 1.2, thus f nilpotent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of formal power series ring A[[x]] (Exercise 1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) f ∈ A[[x]] is a unit ⇐⇒ a0 is a unit in A; (ii) if f is nilpotent then all coefficients are nilpotent (converse false in general); (iii) f ∈ Jacobson radical of A[[x]] ⇐⇒ a0 ∈ Jacobson radical of A; (iv) contraction of a maximal ideal m of A[[x]] is maximal in A and m = m_c + (x); (v) every prime ideal of A is contraction of some prime ideal of A[[x]].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs: explicit recursive formula for inverse series in (i); counterexample for converse of (ii) provided; (v) uses surjectivity behavior in composition of morphisms A → A[[x]] → A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idempotent criterion implies nilradical equals Jacobson radical (Exercise 1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If every ideal not contained in the nilradical contains a nonzero idempotent, then the nilradical and Jacobson radical of A are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses lemma: if e^2 = e is a unit then e =1; if e ∈ R then e=0. Apply Nakayama-type reasoning or the cited Proposition to conclude R(A) ⊂ N(A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rings with x^n = x have prime ideals maximal (Exercise 1.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If every element x in A satisfies x^n = x for some n>1 (possibly depending on x) then every prime ideal in A is maximal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to domain case shows nonzero x either zero or unit; hence domain is field, so primes are maximal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of minimal prime ideals (Exercise 1.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A ≠ 0 then the set of prime ideals of A has minimal elements with respect to inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Zorn's lemma / chain intersection: the intersection of a totally ordered set of primes is prime, hence apply Zorn to obtain minimal primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical ideals are intersections of prime ideals (Exercise 1.9 / Proposition 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal a satisfies a = r(a) iff a is an intersection of prime ideals. The radical r(a) is the intersection of all prime ideals containing a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct consequence of Proposition 1.14: radical equals intersection of primes containing the ideal; converses follow by definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizations of rings with unique prime (Exercise 1.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: For ring A with nilradical N, the following are equivalent: (i) A has exactly one prime ideal; (ii) every element is either a unit or nilpotent; (iii) A/N is a field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard equivalences: unique prime = N is maximal, so nonnil elements are units; conversely quotient by N yields a field when nonnil elements are invertible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boolean ring properties (Exercise 1.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Boolean ring A (x^2 = x for all x): (i) 2x = 0 for all x; (ii) every prime ideal p is maximal and A/p ≅ F2; (iii) every finitely generated ideal is principal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs: algebraic identities; for (iii) construct z = x + y − xy satisfying xz = x, yz = y to show (x,y) = (z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local rings contain no nontrivial idempotents (Exercise 1.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m) is local then A contains no idempotent ≠ 0,1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If e is idempotent and a unit then e=1; else e ∈ m = R and use Lemma 7 to deduce e=0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of algebraic closure (Exercise 1.13, Artin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction: adjoin indeterminates x_f for each irreducible monic polynomial f over K, quotient by ideal generated by f(x_f), take maximal ideal m containing that ideal to get extension K1 = A/m where each f has a root; iterate to obtain algebraic closure L and take algebraic elements over K to get algebraic closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints: show the initial generating ideal ≠ (1) by contradiction with finitely many f_i and evaluating at roots in an extension; show surjectivity at each step and that every f splits in the limit L.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximal elements among ideals consisting of zero-divisors are prime (Exercise 1.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Σ be the set of ideals in which every element is a zero-divisor. Σ has maximal elements and every maximal element of Σ is a prime ideal. Hence the set of zero-divisors is a union of prime ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence via Zorn's lemma (union of chain remains in Σ). Maximality implies primality by same trick as for Proposition 1.8: if a,b ∉ p then p+(a) and p+(b) contain non-zero non-zerodivisors so product ideal p+(ab) does too, hence ab ∉ p, contradiction if p nonprime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zariski closed sets V(E) and Spec topology (Exercise 1.15 & Proposition 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: For X = Spec(A) and E ⊂ A, V(E) = {prime ideals containing E}. Properties: V(E)=V((E))=V(r((E))); V(0)=X, V(1)=∅; arbitrary intersections of V(Ei) correspond to sums/ideals; V(a∩b)=V(ab)=V(a)∪V(b). Proposition 9: bijection between radical ideals and closed subsets of Spec(A) (inverse Y ↦ ⋂_{p∈Y} p), decreasingness, and closure descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These establish the Zariski topology on Spec(A) and the correspondence radical ideals ↔ closed sets. Key propositions and proofs (including contrapositives) are sketched in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic open sets X_f and their properties (Exercise 1.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f ∈ A, X_f = {p ∈ Spec(A) | f ∉ p} is open. Properties: X_f ∩ X_g = X_{fg}; X_f = ∅ ⇐⇒ f nilpotent; X_f = X ⇐⇒ f unit; X_f = X_g ⇐⇒ r((f)) = r((g)); X is quasi-compact; each X_f is quasi-compact; an open subset is quasi-compact iff a finite union of X_f's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use the correspondence between ideals and V(·) and Proposition 9.c (f^n ∈ ideal generated by cover elements). Quasi-compactness arguments rely on finite-generation of ideals appearing in covers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed points and T0 property of Spec (Exercise 1.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) {x} closed ⇐⇒ p_x maximal; (ii) {x} = V(p_x); (iii) y ∈ closure{x} ⇐⇒ p_x ⊂ p_y; (iv) Spec(A) is a T0-space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of primes as points: closed points correspond to maximal ideals. T0 property follows from existence of ideals distinguishing distinct primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreducibility of Spec (Exercise 1.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spec(A) is irreducible ⇐⇒ the nilradical N of A is a prime ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent formulations: closed irreducible subsets are closures of singletons V(p); connect reducibility to existence of ideals a,b with ab ⊂ N but neither contained in N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreducible components (Exercise 1.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any irreducible subspace's closure is irreducible; every irreducible subspace is contained in a maximal irreducible subspace; maximal irreducible subspaces are closed and cover X; for X = Spec(A) irreducible components are V(p) for minimal primes p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard topological facts applied to Spec(A); minimal primes index irreducible components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functoriality of Spec under ring maps (Exercise 1.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: For φ: A → B, induced map φ*: Spec(B) → Spec(A) given by φ*(q) = φ^{-1}(q). Properties: (i) φ*^{-1}(X_f) = Y_{φ(f)} so φ* continuous; (ii) φ*^{-1}(V(a)) = V(ae); (iii) φ*(V(b)) = V(b_c); (iv) surjective φ gives homeomorphism onto V(Ker φ); (v) injective φ ⇒ φ*(Spec(B)) dense in Spec(A) ⇐⇒ Ker φ ⊂ N(A); (vi) functorial composition (ψ∘φ)* = φ*∘ψ*; (vii) example where φ* bijective but not homeomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed equalities given; proofs are routine verifications using preimage/extension/contraction of ideals; the example (vii) shows lack of niceness of MaxSpec functor compared to Spec.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spec of product rings and disconnectedness (Exercise 1.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A = ∏_{i=1}^n A_i then Spec(A) is disjoint union of the Spec(A_i) (each Xi both open and closed). Conversely Spec(A) disconnected ⇔ A ≅ A1 × A2 with nonzero factors ⇔ A contains a nontrivial idempotent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses identification of primes in product rings: primes correspond to prime in one factor and whole of others. Construction of idempotent from decomposition and vice versa is given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boolean rings, clopen sets, and Stone's theorem (Exercises 1.23–1.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) For Boolean ring A, each X_f is both open and closed; finite unions of X_f are again X_g for some g; X_f are the only clopen subsets; X is compact Hausdorff. (2) Boolean lattices correspond to Boolean rings (construction in 1.24). (3) Deduce Stone’s theorem: every Boolean lattice is isomorphic to lattice of clopen subsets of some compact Hausdorff space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints include uniqueness of generators of principal ideals in Boolean rings and lattice-to-ring constructions (a∨b, a∧b and complements). The combination yields the classical Stone duality statement (topological representation of Boolean algebras).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximal spectrum of C(X) recovers X (Exercise 1.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: For compact Hausdorff X, map µ: X → Max(C(X)) sending x ↦ m_x (functions vanishing at x) is a homeomorphism. Consequences: X can be reconstructed from the ring C(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outline: surjectivity uses compactness and partition-of-unity-like argument (sum of squares nonvanishing gives unit contradiction); injectivity uses Urysohn lemma to separate points; topology compatibility via basic opens U_f = {x | f(x) ≠ 0} matching sets {m ∈ Max | f ∉ m}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine varieties and coordinate rings; Nullstellensatz remark (Exercise 1.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given variety X ⊂ k^n defined by polynomials, I(X) = {g | g|_X = 0} is ideal and P(X) = k[t1,...,tn]/I(X) is coordinate ring; points x ↦ m_x give injective map µ: X → Max(P(X)), and surjectivity (µ bijective) is an aspect of Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exercise explains correspondence between points and maximal ideals in coordinate rings; solution deferred but linked to Nullstellensatz in Chapter 7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial maps ↔ algebra homomorphisms (Exercise 1.28)
rubrics_metrics.description: A polynomial mapping φ: k^n → k^m given by f1,...,fm induces a k-algebra homomorphism ψ: k[u1,...,um] → k[t1,...,tn] by ψ(g) = g ∘ φ. Conversely, a k-algebra morphism gives a polynomial map; this gives a bijection between polynomial (regular) maps X → Y and k-algebra homomorphisms P(Y) → P(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given by evaluating coordinate functions and observing natural correspondences; finite/infinite-field caveats noted (exercise assumes k infinite when needed).
